schools.summary: Gill makes the besieger the second of the name and reads the claim on the treasure as possession rather than right.
Henry refers the whole invasion to Israel's apostasy, warns what it costs posterity to bring in a foreign force, and reads the surrender as the effect of sin.
Clarke reports the reading Ben-hadar from the Greek, supposes the submission was calculated to win better terms, and passes on Jarchi's guess about the book of the law.
Ellicott treats the name as an inherited title and the message as an assertion of Syrian overlordship; Keil and Delitzsch call the reply pusillanimous.

debates.question: What did the second demand add to the first?

sides.position: Nothing that can be made out, since the silver, gold, wives and children were already the best he had
The plunder of the whole city, which is a refusal of anything short of unconditional surrender

outliers.note: Alone in reading the surrender as the natural effect of sin, since a king who had provoked God to depart from him had no protection left and had already prepared his silver and gold for Baal.

themes: thirty and two kings with him
thy silver and thy gold is mine
my lord, O king, I am thine
whatsoever is pleasant in thine eyes
1.pericope_label: Benhadad besieged Samaria: thy silver and thy gold is mine

schools.summary: Gill calls the summoning of the elders wisdom in a sneaking spirit, and will not let the refusal itself pass for courage.
Clarke explains the elders' firmness by what they had at stake, and reports the Chaldee reading of the dust-boast as a claim about numbers.

Ellicott hears a threat of destruction in the dust and takes from Josephus the portrait of a drunken braggart; Keil and Delitzsch match the harness proverb with the Latin against singing a triumph too early.

debates.question: What does the boast about the dust of Samaria mean?

sides.position: That the army would be too large for the city's dust to serve the soles of their feet
A threat of destruction as well as a boast, dust being what a razed city becomes

outliers.note: Alone in supplying Josephus's scene, the besieger receiving the reply at a feast, drinking himself drunk, and ordering the assault in one haughty word.

themes: all the elders of the land
hearken not unto him, nor consent
the dust of Samaria shall suffice for handfuls
let not him that girdeth on his harness boast
7.pericope_label: Hearken not unto him; let not him that girdeth on his harness boast

schools.summary: Gill fixes the hour of the drinking as proof of intemperance and doubts that the king went out at the head of his men.
Henry makes security and drunkenness feed each other, compares Belshazzar, and turns the order to take the sallying party alive into the hinge of the battle.
Clarke derives pavilion from the butterfly, reads the word of command as a military term, and makes the young men the royal bodyguard the king was told to lead.
Keil and Delitzsch describe the booths of branches and report Thenius on the section's source; Ellicott dates the re-forming of the prophetic schools and explains Elijah's absence.

debates.question: Who were the young men of the princes of the provinces?

sides.position: The royal bodyguard, the king's own regiment in Samaria
The armour-bearers of the territorial chiefs, picked men and well armed
Pages, few in number and unacquainted with war, which is why they were chosen

outliers.note: Alone in asking whether this unnamed prophet may not be Elijah or Elisha in disguise, since it is strange that neither appears by name.

themes: drinking, he and the kings in the pavilions
there came a prophet unto Ahab
two hundred and thirty two
they went out at noon
12.pericope_label: A prophet came to Ahab: by the young men of the princes of the provinces

schools.summary: Gill keeps the arithmetic that makes the rout marvellous and explains the king's late appearance in the pursuit.
Clarke gives the order to take them alive a practical motive, that prisoners might furnish information, and puts the collapse down to panic.
Ellicott compares the sally with Saul's and Gideon's victories and declines to call it miraculous; Keil and Delitzsch set the governors' servants in front and the army behind.

sides.position: It need not be supposed one, since sudden dispersions of vast Oriental armies are common in history
The slain matched the number of the men who went out against them, which is the wonder of it

outliers.note: Alone in drawing the lesson from Jonathan, that there is no restraint upon the Lord to save by many or by few.

themes: whether they be come out for peace
take them alive
the Syrians fled; and Israel pursued
he smote the horses and chariots
17.pericope_label: They slew every one his man, and the Syrians fled

schools.summary: Gill notes that the warning came from the same prophet and that the proposal assumed Syria could replace its losses.
Henry makes the decree of the end no excuse for neglecting means, itemises the Syrian errors about Jehovah, and draws the contrast of two little flocks of kids against a filled country.
Clarke supplies the military fact under the theology, that broken ground had made the chariots useless, and that the vassal-kings lacked skill.
Ellicott explains tutelary gods from the logic of polytheism and finds policy under the superstition; Keil and Delitzsch name the two alterable causes of the defeat.

debates.question: Why did the Syrians want to fight in the plain?

sides.position: Because the heights and broken ground had made their horses and chariots useless
Because they believed Israel's gods were gods of the hills whose power vanished in the valleys

outliers.note: Alone in noting that organising the tributary kings' troops under the overlord's own officers increased the central power, so that policy lurked under the superstition.

themes: at the return of the year
their gods are gods of the hills
take the kings away, and put captains in their rooms
horse for horse, and chariot for chariot
22.pericope_label: Their gods are gods of the hills; let us fight them in the plain

schools.summary: Gill counts the force unchanged from the year before and explains the week of waiting by the ground each army held.
Clarke places Aphek in Lebanon, reads the promise as God resenting a blasphemy, and offers a burning wind for the fallen wall.

Ellicott offers two sites for Aphek, infers earlier defeats from the smallness of Israel's army, and reads the vindication of God's name before the heathen; Keil and Delitzsch give the slaughter and the wall.

debates.question: How did the wall come to fall on twenty-seven thousand?

sides.position: The Israelites sapped it, or more probably a burning wind did the work
The city wall fell by earthquake or in the storming, the numbers being large as often in this book
The fugitives had climbed the wall to make a stand on it

outliers.note: Alone in reading the episode as a foreshadowing of the prophetic view that all nations have some knowledge of God and stand on probation before him.

themes: he went up to Aphek
like two little flocks of kids
because the Syrians have said
a wall fell upon twenty and seven thousand
26.pericope_label: I will deliver all this great multitude into thine hand

schools.summary: Gill sets out the trap the besieger was caught in, reads the ropes as a token of deserved hanging, and gives the offer of terms to Ahab rather than to Benhadad.
Henry explains the reputation for clemency from the character of Israel's God, and sets the hectoring of the first verses against the whining of these.
Clarke marks the vicissitude of human affairs and follows the grant of streets forward into the origin of European settlements in Asia.
Ellicott reads the word brother as an irrevocable pledge by Eastern custom, and the grant of quarters as a virtual acknowledgment of supremacy.

debates.question: Who offers the terms in the thirty-fourth verse?

sides.position: Ahab, since the name is absent from the original and the kindness is of a piece with the chariot
Benhadad, promising restitution to keep the victor in a favourable mood

outliers.note: Alone in stating the principle breached, that a war conducted under prophetic guidance should not have been concluded without prophetic sanction.

themes: the kings of Israel are merciful kings
let me live
he is my brother
make streets for thee in Damascus
31.pericope_label: Sackcloth on our loins and ropes upon our heads; he is my brother

schools.summary: Gill accepts the identification with Micaiah and notices that the second man was no son of the prophets but a countryman who made no difficulty.
Clarke reads the refusal as a forfeiture that carried the emblem, and defends the lion as proportionate in a man who knew God's ways.
Ellicott explains sonship as discipleship and dates the revival of the schools; Keil and Delitzsch compare the commission with Nathan's symbolic action.

debates.question: What was the self-inflicted wound for?

sides.position: An emblem: as the man died for not smiting when God required it, so the king had forfeited his life for not smiting Benhadad
A symbolic action in Nathan's manner, to make the king pronounce sentence on himself
Hard to account for at all, unless it carried some symbolic application to the king or to Israel

outliers.note: Alone in tracing the institution of the prophetic schools from Samuel's company, and in contrasting the awe these men showed Elijah with their trust in Elisha.

themes: a certain man of the sons of the prophets
smite me, I pray thee
a lion shall slay thee
disguised himself with ashes upon his face
35.pericope_label: Smite me, I pray thee: a certain man of the sons of the prophets

schools.summary: Gill supplies the staging of the roadside cry and has the man speak in the name of the Lord for the greater weight.
Clarke notes where the sentence was executed, distinguishes the king's two words of displeasure, and appends two long excursions on the burning wind and on Calais.
Ellicott groups the parable with Nathan's and the woman of Tekoah's, and gives the fullest account of the fault; Keil and Delitzsch render the charge as the letting go of the man of God's ban.

sides.position: Compassion or weakness standing between God's judgment and its object, since even soft-heartedness may be treason to righteousness
Not smiting an enemy God had put in his hands, and then being displeased with the prophet instead of himself

outliers.note: Alone in arguing from Kennicott that the twenty-seven thousand died under a scorching wind rather than masonry, and in turning the burghers of Calais into a portrait of genuine patriotism.

themes: keep this man
so shall thy judgment be
thy life shall go for his life
heavy and displeased
39.pericope_label: Because thou hast let go a man whom I appointed to utter destruction
